claim: Soviet scientists drilled the Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia for about 20 years, reaching 12,262 m, still inside Earth's crust.
fact_check_evidence: Scientific American: 12,262 m after about 20 years. Other accounts agree the Kola borehole reached 12,262 m in 1989 on the Kola Peninsula and never got beyond the crust. (https://scienceblog.com/t-kola-superdeep-borehole-deepest-vertical-hole/ https://interestingengineering.com/lists/facts-the-superdeep-kola-borehole)

claim: The Kola borehole's 12,262 m is less than 0.2% of the roughly 6,371 km from Earth's surface to its center.
fact_check_evidence: Arithmetic: 12.262 km / 6,371 km = 0.19%. Depth from Scientific American; NASA's Earth Fact Sheet gives a volumetric mean radius of 6,371 km. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_radius https://scienceblog.com/t-kola-superdeep-borehole-deepest-vertical-hole/)

claim: It is about 6,371 km from Earth's surface to its center.
fact_check_evidence: NASA Earth Fact Sheet: volumetric mean radius 6,371.000 km. The globally averaged radius is usually given as 6,371 km. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_radius)

claim: Earth's crust is about 5 to 10 km thick under the oceans and up to 70 km thick under some continents.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: oceanic crust 5 to 10 km; continental crust as thick as 70 km. Britannica: crust varies from a few km to 40 km and up to 70 km in some places. (https://www.britannica.com/science/plate-tectonics/Earths-layers)

claim: The mantle is about 2,900 km thick and makes up about 84% of Earth's volume.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: about 2,900 km thick, 84 percent of Earth's volume. Britannica puts the mantle-core boundary at about 2,900 km depth; other references give 84% of volume. (https://www.britannica.com/science/plate-tectonics/Earths-layers https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_mantle)

claim: Mantle rock is solid, but over long periods it slowly flows, at about the rate fingernails grow.
fact_check_evidence: USGS: a handful of mantle rock would be solid rock, but over long periods it flows slowly at about the rate fingernails grow. NatGeo: mostly solid, moves plastically over millions of years. (https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/mantle/)

claim: Earth's core begins about 2,900 km below the surface and is made almost entirely of iron and nickel.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: the core is about 2,900 km below the surface and almost entirely iron and nickel. Britannica: at about 2,900 km the mantle gives way to an iron-nickel outer core. (https://www.britannica.com/science/plate-tectonics/Earths-layers)

claim: The outer core is liquid iron and nickel, and its swirling motion creates Earth's magnetic field.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: outer core mostly liquid iron and nickel; the magnetic field is created in the swirling outer core. Convection in the liquid outer core drives the geodynamo. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_outer_core)

claim: The inner core is about as hot as the surface of the Sun, yet it stays solid because of the immense pressure of the planet above it.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: inner core reaches about 6,000 C, as hot as the Sun's surface, and stays solid under pressure. Discover and IFLScience report the same. (https://www.discovermagazine.com/earths-inner-core-is-solid-not-liquid-even-though-its-blistering-hot-47785 https://www.iflscience.com/why-is-earths-inner-core-solid-when-its-hotter-than-the-suns-surface-69418)

claim: Earthquake S-waves can't travel through liquid; the shadow where they vanish on Earth's far side revealed the liquid outer core.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: S-waves can't pass through fluids; the shadow where they disappeared showed a liquid layer. IRIS and university texts describe the S-wave shadow zone the same way. (https://www.iris.edu/hq/inclass/animation/seismic_shadow_zone_basic_introduction https://www.uh.edu/~geos6g/1330/interior.html)

claim: The outer core is the only entirely liquid layer inside Earth.
fact_check_evidence: USGS: the only entirely liquid part of Earth's interior is the outer core. NatGeo: the outer core is liquid while the mantle is mostly solid and the inner core solid. (https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/core/)

claim: Tectonic plates move relative to each other at about 2 to 15 cm a year.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: plates move at rates from two to 15 cm a year. USGS: spreading rates range from under 2.5 cm/yr (Arctic Ridge) to over 15 cm/yr (East Pacific Rise). (https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/dynamic/understanding.html)

claim: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreads about 2.5 cm a year; over 100 to 200 million years, the Atlantic grew from a narrow inlet into an ocean.
appears_in: L12 card.world_geography.012.c1; L12 card.world_geography.012.c3; L20 card.world_geography.020.c3
fact_check_evidence: USGS: Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreading averages about 2.5 cm/yr; seafloor spreading over the past 100 to 200 million years grew the Atlantic from a tiny inlet. Britannica: Atlantic widening 1 to 10 cm a year. (https://www.britannica.com/place/Mid-Atlantic-Ridge)

claim: At divergent boundaries, plates pull apart and new crust forms; the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is the best-known example.

fact_check_evidence: USGS: divergent boundaries are where new crust is generated as plates pull away; the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is the best known. Britannica describes seafloor spreading along the ridge's rift. (https://www.britannica.com/place/Mid-Atlantic-Ridge)

claim: At convergent boundaries, plates push together and crust is destroyed as one plate dives under another.
tested_by: L12 question.world_geography.012.q2; L14 question.world_geography.014.q3; L15 question.world_geography.015.q3; L17 question.world_geography.017.q3; L20 question.world_geography.020.q3
fact_check_evidence: USGS: convergent boundaries are where crust is destroyed as one plate dives under another. NatGeo Ring of Fire: plates overlap at convergent boundaries called subduction zones. (https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/ring-fire/)

claim: At transform boundaries, plates slide sideways past each other; California's San Andreas Fault is one.
appears_in: L12 card.world_geography.012.c4; L14 card.world_geography.014.c2; L20 card.world_geography.020.c3
tested_by: L12 question.world_geography.012.q2; L14 question.world_geography.014.q3; L15 question.world_geography.015.q3; L17 question.world_geography.017.q3; L20 question.world_geography.020.q3; L20 question.world_geography.020.q4
fact_check_evidence: USGS: at transform boundaries plates slide horizontally past each other; the San Andreas fault zone is an example. claim: The Pacific Plate slides northwest past the North American Plate about 46 mm a year, so LA and San Francisco will one day be neighbors.
fact_check_evidence: USGS FAQ: Pacific Plate moves northwest relative to North American Plate at about 46 mm a year (the rate fingernails grow); LA and SF will one day be adjacent. USGS This Dynamic Earth gives about 5 cm/yr on the San Andreas. (https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/dynamic/understanding.html)

claim: The San Andreas Fault's plates slide past each other at about the rate your fingernails grow.
fact_check_evidence: USGS FAQ gives about 46 mm a year, 'the rate your fingernails grow'. USGS Earthquake Facts: San Andreas movement averages 3 to 5 cm a year, about the speed fingernails grow. (https://www.usgs.gov/programs/earthquake-hazards/earthquake-facts-earthquake-fantasy)

claim: In 1912, German meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents were once joined in one supercontinent, Pangaea.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: Pangea first proposed in 1912 by German meteorologist Alfred Wegener. USGS: Wegener introduced continental drift in 1912. (https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/continental-drift/)

claim: In 1912, German meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents were once joined in one supercontinent, Pangaea.

claim: The name Pangaea comes from Greek words meaning 'all the Earth'.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: from the Greek pangaia, 'all the Earth'. USGS: Pangaea means 'all lands' in Greek. (https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/dynamic/historical.html)

claim: Pangaea was surrounded by a single global ocean called Panthalassa.

claim: Pangaea began to break apart about 200 million years ago, and its pieces became today's continents.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: began to break apart about 200 million years ago, forming the modern continents. USGS: breakup began about 225 to 200 million years ago. (https://www.livescience.com/38218-facts-about-pangaea.html)

claim: Pangaea began to break apart about 200 million years ago, and its pieces became today's continents.

claim: Most scientists rejected Wegener's idea because he couldn't explain what force could move whole continents.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: the theory lacked a mechanism. USGS: its fatal weakness was that it could not say what forces could move such large masses of rock. claim: Fossils of Mesosaurus, a small freshwater reptile that couldn't have swum the Atlantic, are found only in southern Africa and South America.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: Mesosaurus, a freshwater reptile about 1 m long, could not have swum the Atlantic; fossils only in southern Africa and South America. CK-12 and Wikipedia agree. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesosaur https://www.ck12.org/flexi/earth-science/continental-drift/how-did-wegener-explain-the-presence-of-mesosaurus-fossils-in-africa-and-south-america/)

claim: An earthquake happens when two blocks of Earth suddenly slip past one another along a fault.
fact_check_evidence: USGS: an earthquake is what happens when two blocks of the earth suddenly slip past one another; the surface is the fault. Britannica and BGS and Lumen geology texts describe a sudden slip along a fault releasing stored strain. (https://www.bgs.ac.uk/discovering-geology/earth-hazards/earthquakes/what-causes-earthquakes/ https://courses.lumenlearning.com/geo/chapter/reading-causes-of-earthquakes/)

claim: Rough plate edges get stuck while the rest of the plate keeps moving; when the built-up force beats friction, the rock slips.
fact_check_evidence: USGS: plate edges are rough and get stuck while the rest keeps moving, until the force overcomes friction. Elastic rebound accounts (Lumen, USGS video): a fault stays stuck until strain overcomes friction, then slips suddenly. (https://courses.lumenlearning.com/geo/chapter/reading-causes-of-earthquakes/)

claim: The hypocenter is where an earthquake starts underground; the epicenter is the point on the surface directly above it.
fact_check_evidence: USGS: hypocenter is where the earthquake starts below the surface; epicenter is directly above on the surface. IRIS defines them the same way. (https://www.iris.edu/hq/inclass/video/epicenter_and_focus_hypocenter_of_an_earthquake https://scweb.cwa.gov.tw/en-us/guidance/faqdetail/179)

claim: An earthquake's energy spreads out as seismic waves, like ripples on a pond, and seismographs record them.
fact_check_evidence: USGS: energy radiates outward as seismic waves like ripples on a pond; earthquakes are recorded by seismographs. Lumen geology: the sudden slip releases energy that propagates outward as seismic waves. (https://courses.lumenlearning.com/geo/chapter/reading-causes-of-earthquakes/)

claim: Each whole-number step in earthquake magnitude means ten times bigger swings on a seismogram and about 32 times more energy.
fact_check_evidence: USGS: each whole number is a tenfold increase in measured amplitude and roughly 32 times more energy. PNSN and Minnesota State geology text agree. (https://pnsn.org/education/seismology/magnitude-intensity https://minnstate.pressbooks.pub/environmentalgeology/chapter/magnitude-and-intensity/)

claim: A magnitude 7 earthquake releases about 1,000 times the energy of a magnitude 5 (32 x 32).
fact_check_evidence: Arithmetic from the 32x-per-step rule: 32 x 32 = 1,024, about 1,000. Lumen/PNSN material states a magnitude 7 releases about 1,024 times the energy of a 5. (https://courses.lumenlearning.com/geo/chapter/reading-magnitude-versus-intensity/ https://pnsn.org/education/seismology/magnitude-intensity)

claim: The vast majority of volcanic eruptions and earthquakes happen near plate boundaries.
fact_check_evidence: USGS: the vast majority of earthquakes and volcanic eruptions occur near plate boundaries. NatGeo's Ring of Fire page links most volcanoes to plate boundaries. (https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/ring-fire/)

claim: Where one plate dives beneath another, the sinking rock melts and becomes magma that feeds volcanoes.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: along subduction zones, as rock is subducted it melts and becomes magma. USGS: oceanic-continental convergence sustains many active volcanoes such as the Andes and Cascades. (https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/dynamic/understanding.html)

claim: The Ring of Fire is a string of plate boundaries around the Pacific Ocean about 40,000 km long.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: its length is about 40,000 km and it traces boundaries between plates around the Pacific. Britannica: the horseshoe-shaped belt fringing the Pacific is about 40,000 km long. (https://www.britannica.com/place/Ring-of-Fire)

claim: About 75% of Earth's volcanoes, more than 450, lie along the Ring of Fire, and about 90% of earthquakes happen along it.

claim: Indonesia, made up of some 17,500 islands, has one of the most active volcanic zones in the world, running from Sumatra through Java.

claim: The Philippines, more than 7,000 islands, has about 50 volcanoes, more than 10 of them active.

claim: Hawaii's volcanoes sit mid-plate, more than 3,200 km from the nearest plate boundary, over a stationary hotspot deep in the mantle.

claim: The moving plate carries each Hawaiian island off the hotspot and its volcanoes die out, so the Big Island, still over it, is youngest.

claim: In the open ocean, a tsunami is at most a few meters high, spread over tens to hundreds of kilometers.
fact_check_evidence: USGS: in the open ocean the waves are at most several meters high spread over many tens to hundreds of km. NOAA JetStream: in deep water the top rarely rises more than about three feet above the swell. (https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/tsunamis/tsunami-propagation)

claim: Near shore, a tsunami slows down in the shallower water and builds up higher and higher.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA NOS: waves slow in shallow water and build to higher heights as depth decreases. USGS: amplitude increases as the tsunami approaches shore. (https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/tsunamis/tsunami-propagation)

claim: Near shore, a tsunami slows down in the shallower water and builds up higher and higher.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA NOS: waves slow in shallow water and build to higher heights as depth decreases. USGS: amplitude increases as the tsunami approaches shore. (https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/tsunamis/tsunami-propagation)

claim: Often the first part of a tsunami to reach shore is a trough, so the sea pulls back far from the beach: a natural warning sign.
fact_check_evidence: USGS: the first part of the wave is often a trough, appearing as the sea receding far from shore. NOAA JetStream calls this a common natural warning sign. (https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/tsunamis/tsunami-propagation)

claim: The tsunami from Chile's 1960 earthquake crossed the Pacific in almost 15 hours and killed 61 people in Hilo, Hawaii.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA SOS: almost 15 hours for the first wave to reach Hawaii; it killed 61 in Hilo. NatGeo: the tsunami raced across the Pacific and killed 61 in Hilo. USGS summary lists 61 deaths in Hawaii. (https://www.volcanodiscovery.com/earthquakes/quake-info/2949829/mag9quake-May-22-1960-1960-Great-Chilean-Earthquake-Valdivia-Earthquake.html)

claim: The tsunami from Chile's 1960 earthquake crossed the Pacific in almost 15 hours and killed 61 people in Hilo, Hawaii.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA SOS: almost 15 hours for the first wave to reach Hawaii; it killed 61 in Hilo. NatGeo: the tsunami raced across the Pacific and killed 61 in Hilo. USGS summary lists 61 deaths in Hawaii. (https://www.volcanodiscovery.com/earthquakes/quake-info/2949829/mag9quake-May-22-1960-1960-Great-Chilean-Earthquake-Valdivia-Earthquake.html)

claim: About 80 million years ago, India lay roughly 6,400 km south of Asia, moving north at about 9 m a century.
fact_check_evidence: USGS: about 80 million years ago India was roughly 6,400 km south of Asia, moving north at about 9 m a century. Wikipedia's Indian Plate article gives similar figures. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_plate)

claim: The Himalayas began to form 40 to 50 million years ago, when India collided with Eurasia.
fact_check_evidence: USGS: the range began to form between 40 and 50 million years ago when India and Eurasia collided. USGS plate-motions page also dates the collision to about 50 million years ago. (https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/dynamic/understanding.html)

claim: India and Eurasia have rock of about the same density, so neither could sink under the other; the crust crumpled and thrust upward.
fact_check_evidence: USGS: both landmasses have about the same rock density, so neither could be subducted; the pressure was relieved by thrusting skyward. USGS plate-motions page: the plates crumpled along the collision zone. (https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/dynamic/understanding.html)

claim: The Himalayas are still rising today, because India is still pushing into Asia.
fact_check_evidence: USGS: the collision has yet to end and the Himalayas continue to rise. Science outlets report India still pushing into Eurasia and the range still rising (rates vary by region, so no figure is stated). (https://sciencewatch.blog/why-himalayas-still-growing-taller https://scienceinsights.org/why-are-the-himalayas-still-growing-taller/)

claim: The rock at Everest's summit is limestone that formed on an ancient sea floor, and it holds fossils of sea creatures.
appears_in: L17 card.world_geography.017.c1; L17 card.world_geography.017.c4; L18 card.world_geography.018.c3
fact_check_evidence: IUGS: summit rocks are Ordovician limestones from a shallow sea containing marine fossils. Britannica: the limestone atop Everest was ocean floor with many marine fossils. Montana State's Everest project agrees. (https://www.montana.edu/everest/facts/summit-limestone.html)

claim: The rock at Everest's summit is limestone that formed on an ancient sea floor, and it holds fossils of sea creatures.
appears_in: L17 card.world_geography.017.c1; L17 card.world_geography.017.c4; L18 card.world_geography.018.c3
fact_check_evidence: IUGS: summit rocks are Ordovician limestones from a shallow sea containing marine fossils. Britannica: the limestone atop Everest was ocean floor with many marine fossils. Montana State's Everest project agrees. (https://www.montana.edu/everest/facts/summit-limestone.html)

claim: India's collision with Asia thrust the old sea-floor rock upward to Everest's summit.
fact_check_evidence: IUGS: the rocks were thrust and uplifted into their position when India collided with Asia. USGS: India's collision crumpled the plates and thrust the Himalayas skyward. (https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/dynamic/himalaya.html)

claim: There are three main types of rock: igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: there are three main types of rocks, sedimentary, igneous and metamorphic. USGS and every intro geology text use the same three classes. (https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/what-are-metamorphic-rocks)

claim: Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools and hardens, whether as magma underground or as lava at the surface.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo rock cycle: igneous rocks form when molten material cools and solidifies. NatGeo magma page: magma that has cooled into a solid is igneous rock. (https://opengeology.org/textbook/4-igneous-processes-and-volcanoes/)

claim: Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools and hardens, whether as magma underground or as lava at the surface.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo rock cycle: igneous rocks form when molten material cools and solidifies. NatGeo magma page: magma that has cooled into a solid is igneous rock. (https://opengeology.org/textbook/4-igneous-processes-and-volcanoes/)

claim: Igneous rock that cools slowly underground grows large crystals, like granite; lava that cools fast makes fine-grained rock, like basalt.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: intrusive rocks cool slowly with large crystals, extrusive rocks cool fast and are fine-grained; granite is igneous; mafic lava cools into basalt. OpenGeology and Lumen: granite is coarse-grained intrusive from slow cooling, basalt fine-grained extrusive from fast-cooling lava. (https://opengeology.org/textbook/4-igneous-processes-and-volcanoes/ https://courses.lumenlearning.com/colorado-wmopen-geology/chapter/outcome-igneous-rocks/)

claim: Igneous rock that cools slowly underground grows large crystals, like granite; lava that cools fast makes fine-grained rock, like basalt.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: intrusive rocks cool slowly with large crystals, extrusive rocks cool fast and are fine-grained; granite is igneous; mafic lava cools into basalt. OpenGeology and Lumen: granite is coarse-grained intrusive from slow cooling, basalt fine-grained extrusive from fast-cooling lava. (https://opengeology.org/textbook/4-igneous-processes-and-volcanoes/ https://courses.lumenlearning.com/colorado-wmopen-geology/chapter/outcome-igneous-rocks/)

claim: Sedimentary rock forms from pieces of other rock or once-living material; as layers pile up, the lowest are pressed into solid rock.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: sedimentary rocks form from pieces of other rock or organic material; the lowest layers become compacted into solid rock. USGS and NPS: sediment buried deeply is compacted and cemented into sedimentary rock. (https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/what-are-sedimentary-rocks https://www.nps.gov/subjects/geology/sedimentary.htm)

claim: Limestone is a sedimentary rock often built from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: limestone is sedimentary, its grains often fragments of fossil shells from lime-secreting organisms. AMNH and geology.com describe limestone forming from marine shells and skeletons. (https://www.amnh.org/explore/ology/ology-cards/245-limestone https://geology.com/rocks/limestone.shtml)

claim: Metamorphic rock is rock changed by heat and pressure without melting.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: metamorphic rocks are changed from their original form by immense heat or pressure. USGS: metamorphism does not melt the rocks. (https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/metamorphic-rocks/)

claim: Metamorphic rock is rock changed by heat and pressure without melting.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: metamorphic rocks are changed from their original form by immense heat or pressure. USGS: metamorphism does not melt the rocks. (https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/metamorphic-rocks/)

claim: With enough heat and pressure, limestone turns into marble, and granite turns into gneiss.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo metamorphic rocks: limestone changes into marble; granite under heat and pressure becomes gneiss. NatGeo rock cycle and USGS agree. (https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/rock-cycle/ https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/what-are-metamorphic-rocks)

claim: In the rock cycle, any type of rock can become any other type.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: the rock cycle shows any rock type can become any other. Standard geology texts describe the same cycle between igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rock. (https://flexbooks.ck12.org/cbook/ck-12-middle-school-earth-science-flexbook-2.0/section/4.6/primary/lesson/rocks-and-processes-of-the-rock-cycle-ms-es/ https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/metamorphic-rocks/)

claim: Weathering breaks rock into pieces and erosion carries them away, supplying the sediment that builds sedimentary rock.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo rock cycle: weathering breaks down rock, erosion transports fragments, and accumulated sediment becomes sedimentary rock. NatGeo erosion page defines both processes. (https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/erosion/)

claim: Weathering breaks down or dissolves rock where it sits; erosion wears material away and carries it somewhere else.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: weathering breaks down or dissolves rock but does not involve movement; erosion transports material. Science Notes and other references draw the same distinction. (https://sciencenotes.org/weathering-and-erosion-differences-types-causes-examples/)

claim: Liquid water is the major agent of erosion on Earth; wind and glacial ice erode too.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: liquid water is the major agent of erosion; wind and glaciers also erode. Science Teaching: most erosion is by liquid water, wind or glacial ice. (https://science-teaching.org/science/articles/types-of-erosion)

claim: The Colorado River began carving the Grand Canyon about 5 to 6 million years ago; the canyon is about 1.6 km deep.
fact_check_evidence: NPS geology: the river began carving 5 to 6 million years ago. NPS fly-through: one mile (1.6 km) deep. Live Science and Wikipedia give the same depth and age range. (https://www.livescience.com/27489-grand-canyon.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Canyon)

claim: The Colorado River began carving the Grand Canyon about 5 to 6 million years ago; the canyon is about 1.6 km deep.
fact_check_evidence: NPS geology: the river began carving 5 to 6 million years ago. NPS fly-through: one mile (1.6 km) deep. Live Science and Wikipedia give the same depth and age range. (https://www.livescience.com/27489-grand-canyon.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Canyon)

claim: In floods, the Colorado River carries large rocks that act like chisels, chipping pieces off its bed.
fact_check_evidence: NPS: during floods large rocks and boulders are carried, acting like chisels on the riverbed. EarthDate: floods dragged boulders through the canyon; it is the rocky flood debris, not the water, that does most of the cutting. (https://www.earthdate.org/episodes/carving-a-canyon)

claim: Waves bore caves into sea cliffs; a cave that breaks through becomes an arch, and more wave action leaves rock columns called sea stacks.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: erosion bores caves; when water breaks through the back, it forms an arch; continued wave action leaves sea stacks. Wikipedia and an oceanography text: caves become arches, and eroded arches leave stacks. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stack_(geology) https://rwu.pressbooks.pub/webboceanography/chapter/13-3-landforms-of-coastal-erosion/)

claim: Wind is a powerful agent of erosion: it sculpts rock and piles sand into dunes.
fact_check_evidence: NatGeo: wind is a powerful agent of erosion that sculpts ventifacts and builds sand dunes. NPS: dunes are mounds of sand created by wind; Lumen: wind erosion and deposition shape deserts. (https://www.nps.gov/subjects/geology/aeolian-landforms.htm https://courses.lumenlearning.com/earthscienceck12/chapter/wind-erosion-and-deposition/)

claim: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and is splitting as the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart.
tested_by: L20 question.world_geography.020.q1; L20 question.world_geography.020.q2; L20 question.world_geography.020.q5
fact_check_evidence: USGS: Iceland is splitting along the spreading center between the North American and Eurasian Plates. Museum of Science: Iceland's west and east are the trailing edges of those plates. Wikipedia's Geology of Iceland agrees. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_Iceland)

claim: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and is splitting as the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart.
tested_by: L20 question.world_geography.020.q1; L20 question.world_geography.020.q2; L20 question.world_geography.020.q5
fact_check_evidence: USGS: Iceland is splitting along the spreading center between the North American and Eurasian Plates. Museum of Science: Iceland's west and east are the trailing edges of those plates. Wikipedia's Geology of Iceland agrees. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_Iceland)

claim: Almost all of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is hidden under the sea; Iceland is where it rises above the water.
fact_check_evidence: Museum of Science: the ridge is almost all hidden from view; Iceland is where it can be observed. Wikipedia's Mid-Atlantic Ridge and Guide to Iceland call Iceland the place the ridge is visible above sea level. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Atlantic_Ridge https://guidetoiceland.is/travel-iceland/drive/mid-atlantic-ridge)

claim: At Þingvellir, the land between the separating plates has sunk into a rift valley about 7 km wide.
appears_in: L20 card.world_geography.020.c1; L20 card.world_geography.020.c2; L20 card.world_geography.020.c3
tested_by: L20 question.world_geography.020.q1; L20 question.world_geography.020.q2; L20 question.world_geography.020.q5
fact_check_evidence: Þingvellir National Park: the plates break apart and the land between subsides, in a seven-kilometre wide graben. Wikipedia: the park lies in a rift valley marking the plate boundary. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%9Eingvellir)

claim: In Iceland, the plates move apart about 2 cm a year.
tested_by: L20 question.world_geography.020.q1; L20 question.world_geography.020.q2; L20 question.world_geography.020.q5
fact_check_evidence: Þingvellir National Park: activity away from boundaries is about two centimetres a year. Dive.is and Guide to Iceland give about 2 cm per year at Silfra/Thingvellir. (https://www.dive.is/dive-sites/silfra)

claim: Iceland's volcanoes are also fed by a hotspot beneath the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
tested_by: L20 question.world_geography.020.q1; L20 question.world_geography.020.q2; L20 question.world_geography.020.q5
fact_check_evidence: Museum of Science: hot spot sources feed Iceland's volcanism along the ridge. Wikipedia: Iceland is volcanic because it lies on the ridge and over a hotspot. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland_hotspot)

claim: Water keeps circulating between the ocean, the air and the land, and the total amount of water in the cycle stays essentially constant.
appears_in: L21 card.world_geography.021.c1; L21 card.world_geography.021.c4; L30 card.world_geography.030.c2
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: the total amount of water within the cycle remains essentially constant. NOAA education materials: the total amount of water on Earth stays constant as it changes state. (https://www.noaa.gov/education/resource-collections/freshwater/water-cycle https://www.ck12.org/flexi/earth-science/distribution-of-water-on-earth/the-amount-of-water-on-earth-is-always-changing-or-is-a-constant-amount-true-or-false/)

claim: Energy from the Sun and the force of gravity drive the water cycle.
tested_by: L21 question.world_geography.021.q1; L21 question.world_geography.021.q2; L25 question.world_geography.025.q3; L26 question.world_geography.026.q3
fact_check_evidence: USGS: energy from the sun and the force of gravity drive the continual movement of water. NOAA: the sun drives the water cycle. (https://www.noaa.gov/education/resource-collections/freshwater/water-cycle)

claim: Water evaporates into vapor, condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation such as rain or snow, and moves back across and under the land.
tested_by: L21 question.world_geography.021.q1; L21 question.world_geography.021.q2; L25 question.world_geography.025.q3; L26 question.world_geography.026.q3
fact_check_evidence: USGS describes evaporation, condensation into clouds, precipitation, runoff, streamflow and groundwater. NOAA: water evaporates, condenses into clouds and returns as rain or snow. (https://www.noaa.gov/education/resource-collections/freshwater/water-cycle)

claim: About 90% of the water vapor in the air evaporated from oceans, seas, lakes and rivers; most of the rest came from plants.
fact_check_evidence: USGS: about 90 percent of atmospheric moisture came from oceans, seas, lakes and rivers; the rest from plant transpiration and a little sublimation. Britannica: the principal source of water vapor is the oceans. (https://www.britannica.com/science/water-cycle)

claim: Plants release water vapor through tiny pores in their leaves; this is called transpiration.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: transpiration is the evaporation of water through minute pores, or stomata, in leaves. USGS describes transpiration as water vapor released from plant leaves. (http://usgs.gov/special-topics/water-science-school/science/evapotranspiration-and-water-cycle)

claim: Once it evaporates, a water molecule spends about 10 days in the air on average.
fact_check_evidence: USGS: once evaporated, a water molecule spends about 10 days in the air. Britannica: residence time of water vapor is about 10 days. A Nature Reviews study gives a mean of 8 to 10 days. (https://www.nature.com/articles/s43017-021-00181-9)

claim: Once it evaporates, a water molecule spends about 10 days in the air on average.
fact_check_evidence: USGS: once evaporated, a water molecule spends about 10 days in the air. Britannica: residence time of water vapor is about 10 days. A Nature Reviews study gives a mean of 8 to 10 days. (https://www.nature.com/articles/s43017-021-00181-9)

claim: Seas are smaller than oceans, usually lie where land and ocean meet, and are typically partly enclosed by land.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA: seas are smaller than oceans, located where land and ocean meet, typically partially enclosed by land. Britannica: seas are smaller, shallower and partially enclosed by land. (https://www.britannica.com/science/Ocean-vs-Sea-Whats-the-Difference)

claim: The Sargasso Sea, in the Atlantic, is the only sea with no land boundary; ocean currents alone define its edges.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA: the Sargasso Sea is the only sea without a land boundary, defined only by ocean currents. Wikipedia and Geography Realm agree it is the only sea without a coast. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargasso_Sea https://www.geographyrealm.com/the-only-sea-in-the-world-without-a-coast/)

claim: The ocean's average depth is about 3,700 m.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA: the average depth of the ocean is about 3,682 m. The Natural History Museum and UNESCO Ocean Literacy give about 3,688 m. (https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/quick-questions/how-deep-is-the-ocean.html)

claim: The deepest known point in the ocean, Challenger Deep in the Pacific's Mariana Trench, is about 11 km deep.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA: Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is about 10,935 m deep. The Natural History Museum gives 10,935 m from a 2020 survey. (https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/quick-questions/how-deep-is-the-ocean.html https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_Trench)

claim: Set on the floor of Challenger Deep, Mount Everest would still have its peak about 2 km underwater.
fact_check_evidence: Derived: Challenger Deep about 10,935 m (NOAA) minus Everest about 8,849 m (Britannica) is about 2,086 m. Other science outlets describe the peak as covered by about two kilometers of water. (https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/quick-questions/how-deep-is-the-ocean.html)

claim: Set on the floor of Challenger Deep, Mount Everest would still have its peak about 2 km underwater.
fact_check_evidence: Derived: Challenger Deep about 10,935 m (NOAA) minus Everest about 8,849 m (Britannica) is about 2,086 m. Other science outlets describe the peak as covered by about two kilometers of water. (https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/quick-questions/how-deep-is-the-ocean.html)

claim: In January 1992, a container ship in the North Pacific lost a container holding about 29,000 plastic bath toys.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA JetStream: in January 1992 a container ship lost 12 containers; one held 29,000 bathtub toys. Wikipedia and Smithsonian coverage of oceanographer Curtis Ebbesmeyer give 28,800 toys. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friendly_Floatees_spill)

claim: About ten months later the first toys washed up in Alaska, carried by wind and currents; some later drifted into the Atlantic.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA JetStream: ten months later the first toys washed up in Alaska; driven by wind and currents, some drifted into the Atlantic. Wikipedia: the toys began reaching Alaska at the end of 1992 and some later reached the Atlantic. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friendly_Floatees_spill)

claim: Winds drive the currents at or near the ocean's surface.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA: winds drive currents at or near the ocean surface. NOAA Currents tutorial: large-scale surface currents are driven by global wind systems. (https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/tutorial_currents/04currents2.html)

claim: Ocean currents carry warm water from the Equator toward the poles and cold water from the poles back toward the tropics.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA Ocean Exploration: currents transport warm water from the equator toward the poles and cold water back to the tropics. NOAA: currents drive warm water from the Equator and cold water from the poles. (https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/current.html)

claim: The Gulf Stream is a warm current that flows north along Florida, then turns northeast across the Atlantic.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA: the Gulf Stream is a warm current that moves north along Florida, turns east off North Carolina and flows northeast across the Atlantic. Britannica describes the same path. (https://www.britannica.com/place/Gulf-Stream/Effects-on-marine-and-human-life)

claim: The warm Gulf Stream helps bring milder winters to Bergen, Norway, than to New York, which is much farther south.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA: the warm Gulf Stream brings milder winter weather to Bergen, Norway, than to New York. Fjord Norway and Britannica: the region's winters are milder than elsewhere at that latitude thanks to the Gulf Stream. (https://www.fjordnorway.com/en/inspiration/fjord-norway-in-winter https://www.britannica.com/place/Gulf-Stream/Effects-on-marine-and-human-life)

claim: The Gulf Stream forms the western edge of the Sargasso Sea.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA: the Gulf Stream establishes the Sargasso Sea's western boundary. Wikipedia: the sea is bounded on the west by the Gulf Stream. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargasso_Sea)

claim: Deep currents are driven by differences in density: cold, salty water is dense and sinks, while warm water stays near the surface.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA: thermohaline circulation is driven by density differences due to temperature and salinity; cold, salty water is dense and sinks while warm water stays on the surface. Lumen Earth Science agrees. (https://courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-earthscience/chapter/thermohaline-circulation/)

claim: Deep currents are driven by differences in density: cold, salty water is dense and sinks, while warm water stays near the surface.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA: thermohaline circulation is driven by density differences due to temperature and salinity; cold, salty water is dense and sinks while warm water stays on the surface. Lumen Earth Science agrees. (https://courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-earthscience/chapter/thermohaline-circulation/)

claim: A parcel of water can take about 1,000 years to complete one trip around the ocean's global conveyor belt.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA: it can take 1,000 years for a parcel of water to complete the global conveyor belt. Other oceanography texts give 1,000 to 2,000 years. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermohaline_circulation https://rwu.pressbooks.pub/webboceanography/chapter/9-8-thermohaline-circulation/)

claim: Most ocean waves are caused by wind, through friction between the wind and the water's surface.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA: waves are most commonly caused by wind; wind-driven waves are created by friction between wind and surface water. NOAA JetStream and Smithsonian Ocean agree. (https://ocean.si.edu/planet-ocean/tides-currents/currents-waves-and-tides)

claim: Waves carry energy, not water, across the ocean, and can travel across an entire ocean basin.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA: waves transmit energy, not water, and can travel across an entire ocean basin. CK-12 and other physics sources agree waves carry energy rather than matter. (https://www.ck12.org/flexi/physical-science/forms-of-energy/do-waves-carry-energy-but-not-matter-from-place-to-place/)

claim: Wave erosion can carve a sea arch through rock; when the arch collapses, a sea stack is left standing.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: erosion creates sea arches, and when they collapse a sea stack is left. Wikipedia (Stack) and Internet Geography describe caves eroding into arches that collapse into stacks. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stack_(geology) https://www.internetgeography.net/geotopics/erosion-of-a-headland/)

claim: Further erosion wears a sea stack down until it disappears.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: further erosion wears down the sea stack until it disappears. Wikipedia: continued wave attack undercuts stacks until they collapse into stumps. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stack_(geology))

claim: The Twelve Apostles off Victoria, Australia, are limestone sea stacks; in July 2005 one, about 50 m tall, collapsed into the sea.
fact_check_evidence: ABC News: on 3 July 2005 a 50 m limestone pillar of the Twelve Apostles collapsed. Wikipedia: the Apostles are limestone stacks, and a 50 m stack collapsed in July 2005. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twelve_Apostles_(Victoria))

claim: Waves usually reach a beach at a slight angle, which sets up a longshore current running parallel to the shore.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA: waves arrive at a slight angle and generate a current parallel to the shoreline. LibreTexts oceanography: waves approaching at an angle create longshore currents. (https://geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Oceanography/Oceanography_101_(Miracosta)/12:_Coasts/12.10:_Longshore_Currents_and_Longshore_Drift)

claim: Longshore drift carries beach sand along the shore, and it can cause significant beach erosion.
fact_check_evidence: NOAA: longshore drift transports beach sediment and can cause significant beach erosion. Encyclopedia.com: longshore drift is the transport of sand along a beach by waves breaking at an angle. (https://www.encyclopedia.com/earth-and-environment/ecology-and-environmentalism/environmental-studies/longshore-drift)

claim: The Nile, about 6,650 km long, is usually ranked the world's longest river.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: the Nile, about 6,650 km, is the longest river in the world. National Geographic and Guinness World Records also list the Nile as longest. (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/amazon-longer-than-nile-river)

claim: The Nile flows north through northeastern Africa into the Mediterranean Sea.

claim: Kiribati is made up of 32 atolls and one solitary island.

claim: Wayfinders using the Hawaiian star compass memorize where stars rise and set on the horizon and use those points to find direction.

claim: When the Sun is too high to steer by, wayfinders steer by the ocean swells.

claim: Swells bent around islands and clouds piled up over them can reveal land that is still out of sight.

claim: The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by continents, and its sea ice covers the North Pole.
appears_in: L87 card.world_geography.087.c1; L87 card.world_geography.087.c2; L90 card.world_geography.090.c2
fact_check_evidence: Climate.gov: 'In the Arctic there is an ocean surrounded by continents'; 'Arctic sea ice covers the North Pole.' NSIDC: the Arctic is an ocean basin largely surrounded by land. (https://nsidc.org/learn/ask-scientist/how-does-antarctic-sea-ice-differ-arctic-sea-ice)

claim: Sea ice is frozen ocean water; it forms, grows and melts in the ocean.
fact_check_evidence: NSIDC: 'Sea ice is frozen ocean water. It forms, grows, and melts entirely in the ocean.' NSIDC's Sea Ice overview page gives the same definition. (https://nsidc.org/learn/parts-cryosphere/sea-ice)

claim: Arctic sea ice typically reaches its greatest extent in March and its smallest in September.
fact_check_evidence: NSIDC: the maximum 'typically occurs in March for the Arctic' and the minimum 'typically in September.' NASA's Arctic sea ice minimum indicator tracks the September minimum. (https://science.nasa.gov/earth/explore/earth-indicators/arctic-sea-ice-minimum-extent/)

claim: September Arctic sea ice is shrinking by about 12% per decade, as measured by satellites since 1979.
fact_check_evidence: NASA: 'September Arctic sea ice is shrinking at a rate of 12.2% per decade'; satellite observations started in 1979. NSIDC's 2025 analysis gives a 1979 to 2025 trend of 12.1% per decade. (https://nsidc.org/sea-ice-today/analyses/2025-arctic-sea-ice-minimum-squeezes-ten-lowest-minimums)

claim: Sea ice reflects 50 to 70% of incoming sunlight, while the darker ocean reflects only 6% and absorbs the rest, so losing ice lets the ocean soak up more heat.
fact_check_evidence: NSIDC: 'Sea ice reflects 50 to 70 percent of the incoming energy' while 'the darker ocean reflects only 6 percent of the sun's energy and absorbs the rest.' NSIDC's sea ice overview describes the resulting ice-albedo feedback. (https://nsidc.org/learn/parts-cryosphere/sea-ice)

claim: Antarctica is the world's highest, driest, windiest, coldest and iciest continent.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: 'the world's highest, driest, windiest, coldest, and iciest continent.' The American Museum of Natural History titles its page 'The Coldest, Driest, Windiest, Highest Continent'. (https://www.amnh.org/learn-teach/curriculum-collections/antarctica/the-coldest-driest-windiest-highest-continent)

claim: The lowest temperature ever measured on Earth, −89.2 °C, was recorded at Vostok station in Antarctica on 21 July 1983.
fact_check_evidence: WMO archive lists -89.2 C at Vostok, 21 July 1983 as the world's lowest temperature. Britannica and Wikipedia give the same record (satellite surface readings of about -92 C are not counted). (https://www.britannica.com/science/How-Cold-Does-It-Get-in-Antarctica https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowest_temperature_recorded_on_Earth)

claim: Air gets colder with altitude, so Antarctica's high elevation helps make it colder.
fact_check_evidence: WHOI: 'Since the average elevation of Antarctica is 2.3 km, the air is much colder compared to the Arctic Ocean, which is at sea level.' Discovering Antarctica (BAS/RGS): temperature declines with altitude, so Antarctica's high surface lowers its temperatures. (https://discoveringantarctica.org.uk/oceans-atmosphere-landscape/atmosphere-weather-and-climate/key-factors-behind-antarcticas-climate/)

claim: A desert is defined by low precipitation, usually less than about 250 to 500 mm a year.
fact_check_evidence: Geoscience Australia: a desert 'receives less than 250 to 500 millimetres of precipitation annually.' USGS: desert ecosystems 'receive less than 10 in (250 mm) of annual precipitation.' (https://www.usgs.gov/programs/land-management-research-program/deserts)

claim: Antarctica's snowfall adds up to only about 150 mm of rain a year, making it a cold, dry desert.
fact_check_evidence: BAS: 'Snowfall is equivalent to only 150mm of annual rain.' Britannica: 'The continent is a cold dry desert.' Discovering Antarctica: most of Antarctica is technically a desert. (https://www.britannica.com/place/Antarctica)

claim: Antarctica's snowfall adds up to only about 150 mm of rain a year, making it a cold, dry desert.

claim: Katabatic winds form when air over Antarctica's ice cools, becomes heavier and flows downhill toward the coast.
fact_check_evidence: Australian Antarctic Program: 'The air close to the icy surface cools ... This makes it heavier and forces it to flow downhill'; the flow down to the coast makes the katabatic. Wikipedia's katabatic wind article: dense cold air built up over Antarctica's elevated ice sheets blows out downslope toward the coast. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katabatic_wind)

claim: Antarctica is a rocky continent capped by an ice sheet up to 4.8 km thick.
fact_check_evidence: BAS: 'a rocky continent capped by an ice sheet up to 4.8km thick.' Cool Antarctica: the polar ice cap is 4,800 metres thick at its deepest point. (https://www.coolantarctica.com/Antarctica%20fact%20file/antarctica%20environment/south-pole.php)

claim: The Antarctic ice sheet holds about 90% of the world's ice.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: the ice sheet represents 'about 90 percent of the world's ice.' Wikipedia's Antarctic ice sheet summary: about 90 percent of Earth's total ice volume. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_ice_sheet)

claim: The Antarctic Treaty holds existing claims in place, and no new or enlarged claim can be made while it is in force.

Australian Antarctic Program: nothing done under the Treaty enhances or diminishes claims. (https://www.antarctica.gov.au/about-antarctica/law-and-treaty/history/antarctic-territorial-claims/)

claim: The Antarctic Treaty holds existing claims in place, and no new or enlarged claim can be made while it is in force.

claim: The Antarctic Treaty bans nuclear explosions and the disposal of radioactive waste in Antarctica.

claim: The Antarctic Treaty guarantees freedom of scientific investigation in Antarctica.

claim: The Arctic's ice floats on an ocean that is usually warmer than the air above it, while Antarctica gets little heat from the ocean.

claim: Because Earth's axis is tilted, for six months of the year the Sun never rises over one pole and never sets over the other.
